claim: In familiar environments, the firing fields of entorhinal grid cells form regular triangular lattices.
source: In familiar environments, the firing fields of entorhinal grid cells form regular triangular lattices.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: When the geometric shape of the environment is deformed, time-averaged grid patterns are distorted in a grid scale-dependent and local manner.
source: However, when the geometric shape of the environment is deformed, these time-averaged grid patterns are distorted in a grid scale-dependent and local manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to previous studies (Barry et al., 2007; Stensola et al., 2012) and reanalysis of their data.

claim: Environmental deformations induce boundary-tethered shifts in grid phase that contribute to the appearance of rescaling.
source: We then demonstrated in a computational model that boundary-tethered phase shifts, as well as scale-dependent and local distortions of the time-averaged grid pattern, could emerge from border-grid interactions without altering inherent grid scale.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by reanalysis of experimental data and computational modeling.

claim: The hippocampal formation maintains a metric representation of space that preserves distances between represented locations.
source: The hippocampal formation is thought to maintain a metric representation of space that preserves distances between represented locations, sometimes referred to as a cognitive map (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational work in the field.

claim: Entorhinal grid cells generate the spatial metric via an internally updated, path-integrated representation of space.
source: Entorhinal grid cells are hypothesized to generate this metric via an internally updated, path-integrated representation of space (Hafting et al., 2005; McNaughton et al., 2006; Moser and Moser, 2008; Buzsáki and Moser, 2013; Moser et al., 2014; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The grid representation is most precise when the navigator has recently encountered a boundary.
source: For example, the grid representation is most precise when the navigator has recently encountered a boundary (Hardcastle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hardcastle et al., 2015.

claim: When the environment is moved relative to the broader reference frame of the experimental room, grid phase often remains anchored to the local boundaries.
source: When the environment is moved relative to the broader reference frame of the experimental room, grid phase often remains anchored to the local boundaries (Savelli et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Savelli et al., 2017.

claim: Border cells are co-localized with grid cells in the entorhinal cortex.
source: Co-localized with grid cells in the entorhinal cortex, border cells are active only when a boundary is nearby and at a particular allocentric direction.
evidence: This is a known anatomical fact about border cells.

claim: Border cells are active only when a boundary is nearby and at a particular allocentric direction.
source: Co-localized with grid cells in the entorhinal cortex, border cells are active only when a boundary is nearby and at a particular allocentric direction.
evidence: This is a defining characteristic of border cells.

claim: Border input can be sufficient to reset grid phase and stabilize the grid pattern, provided that border inputs coding for different boundaries map to a consistent allocentric grid phase.
source: Simulations have demonstrated that border input can be sufficient to reset grid phase and stabilize the grid pattern, provided that border inputs coding for different boundaries map to a consistent allocentric grid phase (Hardcastle et al., 2015; Pollock et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to simulation studies.

claim: Stretching or compressing a boundary yields a concomitant rescaling of border activity.
source: stretching or compressing a boundary yields a concomitant rescaling of border activity, displacing a boundary also displaces neighboring border fields, and inserting a new boundary elicits additional border fields at analogous locations neighboring both boundaries (Solstad et al., 2008; Savelli et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Solstad et al., 2008 and Savelli et al., 2008.

claim: Displacing a boundary also displaces neighboring border fields.
source: stretching or compressing a boundary yields a concomitant rescaling of border activity, displacing a boundary also displaces neighboring border fields, and inserting a new boundary elicits additional border fields at analogous locations neighboring both boundaries (Solstad et al., 2008; Savelli et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Solstad et al., 2008 and Savelli et al., 2008.

claim: Inserting a new boundary elicits additional border fields at analogous locations neighboring both boundaries.
source: stretching or compressing a boundary yields a concomitant rescaling of border activity, displacing a boundary also displaces neighboring border fields, and inserting a new boundary elicits additional border fields at analogous locations neighboring both boundaries (Solstad et al., 2008; Savelli et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Solstad et al., 2008 and Savelli et al., 2008.

claim: Grid shift increased along deformed, but not undeformed, dimensions compared to baseline.
source: Compared to this baseline, grid shift increased along deformed, but not undeformed, dimensions (Figure 2A; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of reanalyzed data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Increased shift was observed even in cells with small-scale grid patterns.
source: An increased shift was observed even in cells with small-scale grid patterns (Figure 2B), as well as cells whose time-averaged grid patterns did not appear to rescale (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Increased shift was observed in cells whose time-averaged grid patterns did not appear to rescale.
source: An increased shift was observed even in cells with small-scale grid patterns (Figure 2B), as well as cells whose time-averaged grid patterns did not appear to rescale (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The increase in shift along deformed dimensions was not due to differences in sampling during deformation trials.
source: This increase in shift along deformed dimensions was not due to differences in sampling during deformation trials (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by control analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each boundary rate map is most similar to the familiar environment rate map when the two maps are aligned by the corresponding boundary rather than the opposite boundary.
source: Consistent with the boundary-tethered prediction, we found that the correlation between the deformed environment boundary rate map and the familiar environment rate map was maximized when the two maps were aligned by the corresponding boundary rather than the opposite boundary (313 of 390 comparisons; sign test versus 50%: p<0.001; Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of 390 comparisons.

claim: Boundary-conditioning resulted in a significant reduction in the appearance of rescaling.
source: This analysis revealed a significant reduction in the appearance of rescaling following boundary-conditioning (Figure 3A; Figure 3—source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Field length increased along deformed, but not undeformed, dimensions relative to field length in the familiar environment during compression deformations.
source: This analysis revealed an increase in field length along deformed, but not undeformed, dimensions relative to field length in the familiar environment (Figure 3B; Figure 3—source data 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Peak firing rates were significantly reduced during deformation trials relative to familiar trials.
source: Consistent with the boundary-tethered phase shift prediction, peak firing rates were significantly reduced during deformation trials relative to familiar trials while mean firing rates did not differ significantly (Figure 3C; Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mean firing rates did not differ significantly between deformation and familiar trials.
source: Consistent with the boundary-tethered phase shift prediction, peak firing rates were significantly reduced during deformation trials relative to familiar trials while mean firing rates did not differ significantly (Figure 3C; Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Recorded rate maps were more similar to those predicted by the boundary-tethered model than to those predicted by a matched rescaling.
source: Across cells, recorded rate maps were more similar to those predicted by the boundary-tethered model than to those predicted by a matched rescaling (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—source data 4), as quantified by the correlations between maps (paired t-test comparing Fisher-transformed correlation values: t(132) = 2.95, p=0.004; Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of correlation values shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The border population consisted of 32 units whose activity was designed to mimic the behavior of border cells.
source: The border population consisted of 32 units whose activity was designed to mimic the behavior of border cells (Solstad et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the model architecture.

claim: Each border unit was active only when a boundary was nearby, within 12 cm in a particular allocentric direction.
source: Each border unit was active only when a boundary was nearby, within 12 cm in a particular allocentric direction (Hardcastle et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the model implementation based on Hardcastle et al., 2015.

claim: The model instantiated five grid modules, each consisting of a neural sheet of size 128 × 128 units.
source: The model also instantiated five grid modules, each consisting of a neural sheet of size 128 × 128 units.
evidence: This describes the model architecture.

claim: The internal connectivity and dynamics of each module was based on an attractor model implementing path integration described in Burak and Fiete (2009).
source: The internal connectivity and dynamics of each module was based on an attractor model implementing path integration described in Burak and Fiete (2009), and was identical across modules except for a single movement velocity gain parameter which controlled the grid scale of each module.
evidence: This describes the model implementation based on Burak and Fiete (2009).

claim: The grid patterns of units in large-scale modules rescaled with the environment, but grid patterns of units in small-scale modules tended not to rescale.
source: We found that the grid patterns of units in large-scale modules rescaled with the environment, but grid patterns of units in small-scale modules tended not to rescale (Figure 5B), as observed experimentally (Stensola et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 5B and comparison to experimental data.

claim: During deformations, fields near the displaced wall were distorted, often shifting in concert with the displaced wall, while fields far from this wall were less affected.
source: During deformations, fields near the displaced wall were distorted, often shifting in concert with the displaced wall, while fields far from this wall were less affected (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The correlation between the familiar and deformed environment rate maps was high at locations far from the displaced wall but was reduced near the displaced wall.
source: This correlation was high at locations far from the displaced wall but was reduced near the displaced wall (Figure 5D), indicating that time-averaged grid patterns were distorted near the displaced wall but preserved further away from that wall, as observed experimentally (Krupic et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 5D and comparison to experimental data.

claim: Boundary-tethered shifts in grid phase are observed directly in the activity of recorded grid cells during environmental deformations.
source: Our results support two primary conclusions. First, boundary-tethered shifts in grid phase are observed directly in the activity of recorded grid cells during environmental deformations, and contribute to the appearance of rescaling.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by reanalysis of experimental data.

claim: Boundary-tethered shifts in grid phase, scale-dependent rescaling, and local distortions of the time-averaged grid pattern can emerge from border cell-grid cell interactions.
source: Second, boundary-tethered shifts in grid phase, scale-dependent rescaling, and local distortions of the time-averaged grid pattern can emerge from border cell-grid cell interactions.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by computational modeling.

claim: Time-averaged analyses may have overestimated the malleability of the grid cell spatial metric in response to environmental deformations.
source: These results further indicate that time-averaged analyses may have overestimated the malleability of the grid cell spatial metric in response to environmental deformations and suggest that scale-dependent grid rescaling may not be a clear indicator of a functional dissociation between modules.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results based on the finding that boundary-tethered shifts contribute to the appearance of rescaling.

claim: Scale-dependent grid rescaling may not be a clear indicator of a functional dissociation between modules.
source: These results further indicate that time-averaged analyses may have overestimated the malleability of the grid cell spatial metric in response to environmental deformations and suggest that scale-dependent grid rescaling may not be a clear indicator of a functional dissociation between modules.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results based on the model showing that a single mechanism can produce both rescaling and non-rescaling patterns.

claim: The effects of environmental deformations are not fixed over time, but instead depend crucially on the movement history of the navigator.
source: Finally, these results demonstrate that the effects of environmental deformations are not fixed over time, but instead depend crucially on the movement history of the navigator.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the finding that grid phase shifts depend on which boundary was most recently encountered.

claim: In Barry et al., 2007, rats were familiarized with either a 100 cm x 100 cm square or a 100 cm x 70 cm rectangular open environment.
source: In Barry et al., 2007), rats were familiarized with either a 100 cm x 100 cm square or a 100 cm x 70 cm rectangular open environment, and then reintroduced to deformed and undeformed versions of these environments (i.e. all combinations of chamber lengths and widths of 70 cm or 100 cm), while the activity of grid cells was recorded (familiar square: 23 grid cells; familiar rectangle: 13 grid cells meeting criteria; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental design from Barry et al., 2007.

claim: In Stensola et al. (2012), rats were familiarized with a 150 cm x 150 cm square open environment.
source: In Stensola et al. (2012), rats were familiarized with a 150 cm x 150 cm square open environment, and then reintroduced to deformed (100 cm x 150 cm rectangular) and undeformed versions of this environment, while data were recorded from 51 grid cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental design from Stensola et al., 2012.

claim: The time-averaged grid patterns of most grid cells appeared to rescale when the environment was deformed, though the grid patterns of a subset of cells with smaller grid scales did not.
source: As previously reported (Barry et al., 2007; Stensola et al., 2012), the time-averaged grid patterns of most of these grid cells appeared to rescale when the environment was deformed, though the grid patterns of a subset of cells with smaller grid scales did not.
evidence: This summarizes findings from previous studies.

claim: Boundary contact was defined as coming within 12 cm of a boundary.
source: First, we separated the spiking data of each cell according to the most recently contacted boundary, either the north, south, east or west, with contact defined as coming within 12 cm of that boundary (Hardcastle et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the analysis method used, based on Hardcastle et al., 2015.

claim: Comparison of boundary rate maps conditioned on contact with opposing boundaries revealed clear examples of grid shift along deformed dimensions.
source: Comparison of such rate maps, conditioned on contact with opposing boundaries (north-south vs. east-west), revealed clear examples of grid shift along deformed dimensions (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual examples shown in Figure 1.

claim: If the deformation extent is less than the grid period then different boundaries will reinstate different phases, resulting in a time-averaged grid pattern which appears rescaled.
source: Generally, if the deformation extent is less than the grid period then different boundaries will reinstate different phases, resulting in a time-averaged grid pattern which appears rescaled.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model about how scale-dependent rescaling emerges.

claim: When the deformation extent nearly matches the grid period, different boundaries will reinstate a similar phase, yielding a largely undistorted time-averaged pattern.
source: When the deformation extent nearly matches the grid period, different boundaries will reinstate a similar phase, yielding a largely undistorted time-averaged pattern.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model about how scale-dependent rescaling emerges.

claim: When the deformation extent exceeds the period, different boundaries will again reinstate different phases; thus, the time-averaged pattern will appear distorted but will not resemble a simple rescaling of the grid to match the deformation.
source: When the deformation extent exceeds the period, different boundaries will again reinstate different phases; thus, the time-averaged pattern will appear distorted. However, in the latter case, additional fields will appear (during stretches) or previously-observed fields will disappear (during compressions). Therefore, the time-averaged pattern, although distorted, will not resemble a simple rescaling of the grid to match the deformation.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model about how scale-dependent rescaling emerges.

claim: Whether or not the grid patterns of a particular module appear to rescale is not an inherent property of the module, but rather an interaction between the grid scale and deformation extent.
source: In addition to capturing scale-dependent rescaling, this model further predicts that whether or not the grid patterns of a particular module appear to rescale is not an inherent property of the module, but rather an interaction between the grid scale and deformation extent.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model based on the mechanism of boundary-tethered shifts.

claim: Modules with periods less than or equal to the deformation extent will tend not to resemble a rescaling.
source: Specifically, modules with periods less than or equal to the deformation extent will tend not to resemble a rescaling, consistent with the data in (Stensola et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model that is consistent with experimental data.

claim: A grid with a given scale can appear to rescale during less extreme but not during more extreme deformations.
source: Moreover, this model predicts that a grid with a given scale can appear to rescale during less extreme but not during more extreme deformations, consistent with comparison across experiments (Barry et al., 2007; Stensola et al., 2012; Savelli et al., 2008) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model that is consistent with comparison across experimental studies.

claim: A single mechanism is capable of simultaneously reproducing the appearance and absence of rescaling across modules.
source: Finally, this model demonstrates that a single mechanism is capable of simultaneously reproducing the appearance and absence of rescaling across modules, suggesting that the extent of rescaling may not be clear evidence of a functional dissociation between modules (Stensola et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model simulations.

claim: Time-averaged grid fields near a boundary will appear less distorted than central fields during stretching and compression deformations.
source: Because of these biases, time-averaged grid fields near a boundary will appear less distorted than central fields during stretching and compression deformations.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the interaction between boundary-tethered shifts and sampling biases.

claim: The most recently encountered boundary is correlated with the direction of movement.
source: Relatedly, the most recently encountered boundary is also correlated with the direction of movement – a given boundary is more likely to have been recently encountered when moving away from that boundary (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of movement patterns shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Boundary-tethered shifts in grid phase are predicted to resemble modulation by movement direction, analogous to similar modulation observed in place cells.
source: Thus, boundary-tethered shifts in grid phase are also predicted to resemble modulation by movement direction, analogous to similar modulation observed in place cells (O'Keefe and Burgess, 1996).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the correlation between most recently encountered boundary and movement direction, with reference to similar effects in place cells.

claim: Sampling biases play a critical role in mediating the contribution of boundary-tethered shifts to distortions of the time-averaged grid pattern.
source: Thus, in this model sampling biases, a product of the particular path of the navigator, play a critical role in mediating the contribution of boundary-tethered shifts to distortions of the time-averaged grid pattern.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model about the role of sampling biases.

claim: Simple interactions between border cells and grid cells are sufficient to reproduce boundary-tethered shifts in grid phase.
source: Through our simulations, we have demonstrated that simple interactions between border cells and grid cells are sufficient to reproduce boundary-tethered shifts in grid phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the computational modeling.

claim: Visual inputs play important roles in developing and maintaining a functional grid code.
source: For example, visual inputs (Pérez-Escobar et al., 2016) and reciprocal connections from place to grid cells (Bonnevie et al., 2013) both play important roles in developing and maintaining a functional grid code, and may contribute to phase anchoring during deformations (Sheynikhovich et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Reciprocal connections from place to grid cells play important roles in developing and maintaining a functional grid code.
source: For example, visual inputs (Pérez-Escobar et al., 2016) and reciprocal connections from place to grid cells (Bonnevie et al., 2013) both play important roles in developing and maintaining a functional grid code, and may contribute to phase anchoring during deformations (Sheynikhovich et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Similar boundary-tethered dynamics can be observed in the place code even before the grid code has fully matured.
source: Moreover, similar boundary-tethered dynamics can be observed in the place code even before the grid code has fully matured, suggesting that additional mechanisms may contribute to similar dynamics in place cells (Bjerknes et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bjerknes et al., 2018.

claim: Grid scale differs between novel and familiar environments.
source: For example, grid scale differs between novel and familiar environments (Barry et al., 2012), the grid pattern is anchored both by spatial geometry and other visual features (Savelli et al., 2017; Krupic et al., 2015), and the grid pattern distorts near familiar boundaries as well as in asymmetric environments (Krupic et al., 2015; Stensola et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barry et al., 2012.

claim: The grid pattern is anchored both by spatial geometry and other visual features.
source: For example, grid scale differs between novel and familiar environments (Barry et al., 2012), the grid pattern is anchored both by spatial geometry and other visual features (Savelli et al., 2017; Krupic et al., 2015), and the grid pattern distorts near familiar boundaries as well as in asymmetric environments (Krupic et al., 2015; Stensola et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Savelli et al., 2017 and Krupic et al., 2015.

claim: The grid pattern distorts near familiar boundaries as well as in asymmetric environments.
source: For example, grid scale differs between novel and familiar environments (Barry et al., 2012), the grid pattern is anchored both by spatial geometry and other visual features (Savelli et al., 2017; Krupic et al., 2015), and the grid pattern distorts near familiar boundaries as well as in asymmetric environments (Krupic et al., 2015; Stensola et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Krupic et al., 2015 and Stensola et al., 2015.

claim: During deformations the distorted grid pattern does not persist indefinitely, but relaxes back to the familiar spatial scale with experience.
source: For example, it is known that during deformations the distorted grid pattern does not persist indefinitely, but relaxes back to the familiar spatial scale with experience (Barry et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barry et al., 2007.

claim: In the model, weights were fixed during deformation trials so that no further learning occurred in this phase.
source: However, in our simulations, model weights were fixed during deformation trials so that no further learning occurred in this phase.
evidence: This describes a feature of the model implementation.

claim: Recent evidence suggests that rescaling can be observed in the time-averaged activity of human grid cells.
source: Consistent with this idea, recent evidence suggests that rescaling can be observed in the time-averaged activity of human grid cells (Nadasdy et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nadasdy et al., 2017.

claim: Boundary-tethered grid shift may be a common mechanism contributing to cross-species effects in spatial memory during environmental deformations.
source: In light of our results and further simulations of place cell activity (see Materials and methods), we suggest that boundary-tethered grid shift may be a common mechanism contributing to these cross-species effects, and predict that similar boundary-tethered shifts should be observed in human spatial memory during environmental deformations.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the results and simulations, with a prediction for future research.

claim: Similar boundary-tethered shifts should be observed in human spatial memory during environmental deformations.
source: In light of our results and further simulations of place cell activity (see Materials and methods), we suggest that boundary-tethered grid shift may be a common mechanism contributing to these cross-species effects, and predict that similar boundary-tethered shifts should be observed in human spatial memory during environmental deformations.
evidence: This is a prediction for future research based on the current findings.

claim: The preferred firing field of each border unit covered 50% of the length of one side of the environment.
source: The preferred firing field of each border unit covered 50% of the length of one side of the environment.
evidence: This describes the model implementation.

claim: Fields maintained proportional coverage when the preferred boundary was deformed.
source: Fields maintained proportional coverage when the preferred boundary was deformed (Pollock et al., 2018; Solstad et al., 2008; Savelli et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the model implementation based on previous research.

claim: During familiarization, excitatory connections from border units to coactive grid units were strengthened at the expense of non-coactive connections.
source: During familiarization, these connections developed through experience via a Hebbian learning rule in which connections between coactive grid and border units were strengthened at the expense of connections from inactive border units (Grossberg, 1980) (Figure 4B; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the model implementation based on Grossberg, 1980.

claim: Once familiarized, border unit input acted to reinstate the grid network state associated with the same pattern of border unit responses during familiarization.
source: Once familiarized, border unit input acted to reinstate the grid network state associated with the same pattern of border unit responses during familiarization.
evidence: This describes the behavior of the model after familiarization.

claim: Grid reinstatement occurred even when border inputs were activated at a new location, such as when a displaced boundary was encountered.
source: This grid reinstatement occurred even when border inputs were activated at a new location, such as when a displaced boundary was encountered.
evidence: This describes the behavior of the model during deformations.

claim: In a rescaled environment, grid reinstatement led to shifts in grid phase, such that the phase relative to the most recent border input matched the phase entrained during familiarization in the undeformed environment.
source: In a rescaled environment, this grid reinstatement led to shifts in grid phase, such that the phase relative to the most recent border input matched the phase entrained during familiarization in the undeformed environment (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This describes the behavior of the model during deformations, shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Averaged over time, boundary-tethered shifts in grid phase can resemble a rescaling.
source: Averaged over time, these shifts in grid phase can resemble a rescaling (Figure 4E).
evidence: This describes the behavior of the model, shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Stretching a familiar environment induces a heterogeneous mix of responses in the time-averaged activity of place cells.
source: Electrophysiological experiments have shown that stretching a familiar environment induces a heterogeneous mix of responses in the time-averaged activity of place cells (O'Keefe and Burgess, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to O'Keefe and Burgess, 1996.

claim: A number of place units exhibited place field stretching in proportion to the rescaling deformation.
source: A number of place units exhibited place field stretching in proportion to the rescaling deformation.
evidence: This describes the behavior of modeled place units during deformations.

claim: Some place units exhibited place field bifurcations accompanied by progressively lower peak firing rates during more extreme deformations.
source: Other units exhibited place field bifurcations accompanied by progressively lower peak firing rates during more extreme deformations.
evidence: This describes the behavior of modeled place units during deformations.

claim: Some place units exhibited emergent modulation by movement direction, with place fields shifting 'upstream' of the movement direction.
source: Finally, some units exhibited emergent modulation by movement direction, with place fields shifting 'upstream' of the movement direction.
evidence: This describes the behavior of modeled place units during deformations.

claim: When a familiar linear track is compressed, the place code is updated when track ends are encountered.
source: Electrophysiological experiments have also demonstrated that when a familiar linear track is compressed, the place code is updated when track ends are encountered (Gothard et al., 1996; Gothard et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gothard et al., 1996 and Gothard et al., 2001.

claim: During laps on compressed tracks, place unit activity unfolded as if unaffected by the compression until the opposing track end was reached.
source: During laps on compressed tracks, place unit activity unfolded as if unaffected by the compression, no matter how extreme, until the opposing track end was reached.
evidence: This describes the behavior of modeled place units during linear track compressions.

claim: Once the opposing track end was encountered, the place code previously active at this track end during familiarization reemerged.
source: Once encountered, the place code previously active at this track end during familiarization reemerged (Figure 7B), as observed experimentally (Gothard et al., 1996).
evidence: This describes the behavior of modeled place units during linear track compressions, shown in Figure 7B and consistent with experimental data.

claim: When a boundary is inserted in a familiar open environment, place fields exhibit a mix of duplication, suppression, and perseverance.
source: Finally, electrophysiological experiments have shown that when a boundary is inserted in a familiar open environment, place fields exhibit a mix of duplication, suppression, and perseverance (Barry et al., 2006; Muller and Kubie, 1987; Lever et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barry et al., 2006, Muller and Kubie, 1987, and Lever et al., 2002.

claim: Some modeled place units exhibited place field duplication during boundary insertion.
source: Some units exhibited place field duplication during boundary insertion, while other units exhibited place field inhibition.
evidence: This describes the behavior of modeled place units during boundary insertions.

claim: Some modeled place units exhibited place field inhibition during boundary insertion.
source: Some units exhibited place field duplication during boundary insertion, while other units exhibited place field inhibition.
evidence: This describes the behavior of modeled place units during boundary insertions.

claim: Some modeled place units persevered largely unaffected during boundary insertion.
source: Still others persevered largely unaffected.
evidence: This describes the behavior of modeled place units during boundary insertions.

claim: Many of the heterogeneous place cell behaviors observed across environmental deformations could arise from boundary-tethered shifts in grid code input.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that many of the heterogeneous place cell behaviors observed across environmental deformations could arise from boundary-tethered shifts in grid code input.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the place cell simulations.

claim: Data from Barry et al., 2007 included 36 grid cells meeting the inclusion criteria of average gridness across both familiar trials > 0.4.
source: Data from Barry et al., 2007) included an initial set of 66 putative cells, from which 38 cells meeting various criteria were selected as grid cells for analysis in the original publication. Similarly, we included only cells with average gridness across both familiar trials > 0.4 from this dataset, yielding 36 included grid cells.
evidence: This describes the data selection criteria for the reanalysis.

claim: Cells which were poorly fit by rescaling during deformation trials were not excluded from the reanalysis.
source: Note that unlike in Barry et al., 2007) we did not exclude cells which were poorly fit by rescaling during deformation trials, as boundary-tethered phase shifts predict that distortions which do not resemble a rescaling may occur.
evidence: This describes a difference in data selection criteria between the original study and the reanalysis.

claim: Only the spikes from 30 randomly chosen grid units in each module were recorded and analyzed during all simulations due to computational constraints.
source: Due to computational constraints and the redundant nature of grid unit activity, only the spikes from 30 randomly chosen grid units in each module were recorded and analyzed during all simulations.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the computational simulations.

claim: Rate maps were created by dividing the environment into 2.5 cm x 2.5 cm pixels and calculating the mean firing rate within each pixel.
source: Rate maps were created by first dividing the environment into 2.5 cm x 2.5 cm pixels. Then the mean firing rate within each pixel was calculated.
evidence: This describes the method for creating rate maps.

claim: Rate maps were smoothed with an isotropic Gaussian kernel with a standard deviation of 1.5 pixels (3.75 cm) and square extent of 9 pixels x 9 pixels (22.5 cm x 22.5 cm).
source: Finally, this map was smoothed with an isotropic Gaussian kernel with a standard deviation of 1.5 pixels (3.75 cm) and square extent of 9 pixels x 9 pixels (22.5 cm x 22.5 cm).
evidence: This describes the method for smoothing rate maps.

claim: Grid scale was computed as the mean distance from the center of the autocorrelation to the center of mass of the six closest surrounding peaks, excluding the central peak.
source: To compute grid scale for a unit or cell we first computed the rate map autocorrelation. Next, we computed the mean distance from the center of the autocorrelation to the center of mass of the six closest surrounding peaks, excluding the central peak.
evidence: This describes the method for computing grid scale.

claim: Gridness was computed as the difference between the minimum of the [60° 120°] correlations minus the maximum of the [30° 90° 150°] correlations of the masked autocorrelation.
source: The final measure of gridness was then the difference between the minimum of the [60° 120°] correlations minus the maximum of the [30° 90° 150°] correlations.
evidence: This describes the method for computing gridness.
